f-indemn-458baee3.reason: The redline does not achieve either position. Its central defect is structural: Section 14.1 is changed to reference cases “(a) through (d),” but no substantive paragraph (d) is placed within Section 14.1. Instead, paragraph (d) follows Section 14.2(a), whose introductory language makes Sanofi the indemnitor and RevMed the indemnitee. The addition therefore creates a Customer-to-Vendor IP indemnity—the opposite of the intended Vendor-to-Customer protection. It also omits the preferred law, data-breach, procedure, and limited Customer-indemnity requirements, as well as the fallback specification exclusion, infringement remedies, and 3× annual-fees super-cap. The reversed indemnity direction introduces a material contradiction and expands Customer's liability.

f-lol-cap-71b0bce3.reason: The clause reaches the fallback because it provides a mutual cap incorporating a twelve-month payment benchmark and uncaps indemnification, confidentiality, gross negligence, and wilful misconduct. It does not reach the preferred position: data protection and security carve-outs are absent; the lookback is tied to the event giving rise to the claim rather than the claim; the IP language does not demonstrably cover infringement of the other party's IP; and the operative language does not establish that Sanofi is the Customer for the payment-obligations treatment. The amendments are confined to liability-cap concepts and preserve unrelated terms, but drafting quality is reduced by the duplicated indemnification/confidentiality/IP proviso and the foregoing scope ambiguities.

f-t4c-fdb17917.reason: Neither level is fully satisfied. The central defect is party direction: the Issuer may terminate only at the Depositor's direction, rather than having an independent Customer right. The fallback also fails because the notice period is 30 days rather than 60–90 days. The refund, absence of an early-termination fee, and prohibition on Vendor convenience termination are otherwise protective. The redline is not minimal because it adds partial-termination authority, additional notice recipients, fee-waiver language, successor-servicer mechanics, and resignation-related language beyond what was necessary. It generally preserves the existing servicing and transaction-document structure, but “in whole or in part” may interact awkwardly with successor-servicer provisions designed for a complete removal.
